62: VA duty to notify and assist: the veteran argued the VA failed to adequately investigate his claims that his sentence had been vacated. The court held the VA had no duty to investigate further because changes in sentence do not end the reduction period.

In any event, changes in sentence do not warrant resumption of benefits under § 5313(a)(1). A veteran's compensation reduction does not end until the incarceration ends. The VA therefore had no obligation to conduct any further investigation.
132: Due process notice: whether VA must give notice that a referral to a private facility could affect § 1151 benefits; the court held there is no due process right to such notice and affirmed.
Accordingly, we affirm the Veterans Court's decision on Mr. Ollis's due process claim.
159: Duty to assist: VA must determine all potential claims raised by the evidence, including TDIU, regardless of whether the claim is labeled as TDIU; the Board's mootness determination was wrong.
Here, the Mr. Palmatier placed the VA on notice on multiple occasions.
1051: Whether the Final Rule's requirements for claimants to identify symptoms, conditions and issues violate the VA's duty to develop claims and the benefit-of-the-doubt rule under 38 U.S.C. § 5107; held a permissible construction.

we find that new 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.160(a)(3)–(4) and 19.24(b) of the VA's Final Rule requiring that claimants identify symptoms or medical conditions at a high level of generality is a permissible construction of the statute.
1089: Whether the Board and Veterans Court were bound to presume the competence of a VA medical examiner under the Rizzo line of precedent, as part of the VA's duty to assist; the court declined to disavow the presumption and affirmed.

We lack jurisdiction to make factual findings on appeal regarding the competency of the particular examiner employed by the VA in this case and are bound by clear precedent to presume that Dr. Dudek was competent to render the opinion he did.
1328: VA procedural error in failing to take action on the Board-referred claim, denying due process and the opportunity to develop the record
We hold that the VA committed procedural error by failing to take action on the claim that was referred to it by the Board.
1631: Due process notice and opportunity to be heard in a VA special monthly compensation claim; court found no denial of due process where VA gave notice of the examination consequence and several chances to explain non-attendance.
We find no denial of due process.
1949: Benefit of the doubt rule under 38 U.S.C. 5107(b): Board found no approximate balance of evidence, a factual finding the court accepted
Here, however, the Board did not find that there was such an approximate balance.
2113: Adequacy of Board notice to claimant's counsel of the 90-day deadline for submitting new evidence on remand; Veterans Court erred in holding the notice defect was cured, and the error was not harmless.
In these circumstances, we conclude that the Veterans Court legally erred in finding a cure of the notice defect.
2204: Whether application of the implicit denial rule violates the VA due process regulation's notice provision (38 C.F.R. 3.103(e)); court held the 1985 decision gave adequate notice, so no violation.
Accordingly, the application of the implicit denial rule does not violate Mr. Cogburn's right to receive notice pursuant to the VA's due process regulation.
2792: Notice and implicit denial: the court held implicit denial requires adjudication and notice to the veteran, so the government cannot treat an unrecognized claim as implicitly denied.
Implicit denial requires adjudication. It does not shield the government from failure to adjudicate.
3054: Duty to assist under 38 U.S.C. § 5103A: the court held that § 5103A does not restrict the Board's authority to order a medical examination beyond the statute's affirmative duty, rejecting the veteran's argument that the Board had to make an adequately explained finding of insufficiency before ordering one.
We hold that § 5103A contains no such requirement.
3129: Benefit of the doubt doctrine under 38 U.S.C. 5107(b) does not help claimant because it cannot change the statutory definition of period of war
The "benefit of the doubt" doctrine does not help Mr. Lamm, as the doctrine cannot serve to change Congress's definition of "period of war."
3150: Whether VA provided proper notice of the time limits for filing an NOA and a motion for reconsideration, and whether the notice attachment (VA Form 4597) was adequate; the court found proper notice was given.

Because Mr. Helm received proper notice of the time for filing both an NOA and a motion for reconsideration, and because he has failed to show how his misunderstanding of such notice constitutes extraordinary circumstance or how the inclusion of a statement informing him of the Amendment caused the untimely filing of his motion for reconsideration, the doctrine of equitable tolling does not apply.
3289: Duty to notify and equitable tolling: whether the government's failure to notify the veteran of benefit eligibility tolls the effective-date rule
And we have previously rejected similar equitable arguments.
3417: Benefit-of-the-doubt rule under 38 U.S.C. § 5107(b): court held the rule did not apply because the evidence was not in approximate balance and the Board found the preponderance weighed against the veteran.
There was no error in not applying the "benefit of the doubt" doctrine.
3522: Duty to assist: propriety of the April 2014 addendum VA examination addressing direct service connection; court found no error in VA conducting it or the BVA's treatment of it.
we discern no error in the VA's conducting that examination or the BVA's treatment thereof.
3560: Benefit-of-the-doubt rule (38 U.S.C. 5107(b)) does not apply to CUE motions.

The benefit of the doubt rule does not apply in the context of CUE motions, however, because CUE is an error where there can never be a balance of the evidence situation in which there must be benefit of the doubt in favor of the veteran.
4099: Notice of the Board decision via mailing under 38 U.S.C. § 7104(e): the court rejected the argument that the VA must present direct evidence of mailing and held circumstantial evidence of mailing procedures sufficient, so notice was properly given.
It is well established that circumstantial evidence (here, evidence of the VA’s mailing procedures) can be sufficient to prove a fact; direct evidence is not necessary.
4137: Scope of the VA duty to assist; the court held the duty to assist is triggered only by a formal claim that identifies the medical condition, rejecting Sellers' argument that the duty requires searching records for unclaimed conditions.
The former is necessary to initiate the latter.
6060: Duty to assist: whether the Veterans Court applied an impermissibly high threshold to trigger VA's duty to assist in obtaining VA treatment records (38 U.S.C. 5103A; relevance limitation under 38 CFR 3.159(c)(3))
We agree with Ms. Jones that the Veterans Court erred as a matter of law in requiring an impermissibly high threshold to trigger the VA's duty to assist.
6128: Whether the VA's differing regulatory treatment of ALS versus C-123 and Camp Lejeune situations was arbitrary and capricious under 38 U.S.C. 7292(d)(1)
Mrs. Hansen-Sorensen has not made a persuasive showing of arbitrariness on such grounds in this matter.
6357: Whether the presumption of competency of VA medical examiners is consistent with the VA's duty to assist and the benefit-of-the-doubt rule; court held the presumption applies unless the veteran raises a competency challenge.
The presumption of competency requires nothing more than is required for veteran claimants in other contexts—simply a requirement that the veteran raise the issue.
6579: Pro-veteran canon and the duty-to-assist 'no reasonable possibility' standard of 38 U.S.C. § 5103A(a)(2); court held the pro-veteran canon does not apply absent interpretive doubt and the duty to assist does not extend to records that do not establish a missing element.
Mr. Kisor argues that we should resort to the pro-veteran canon of construction ... The canon therefore does not apply here.
6861: Whether VA may rely on the Army's service determination for Filipino Veterans Equity Compensation Fund eligibility without giving the claimant a meaningful opportunity to challenge her service record (duty to assist/notice).

But we further held that in this particular context, the VA cannot rely on the service department's determination without giving the veteran a meaningful opportunity to challenge his or her service record.
6900: Whether failure to apply statutory presumptions of soundness and service connection is per se prejudicial; court held harmless-error analysis applies, no per se rule of prejudice
We therefore hold that a per se rule of prejudice is not appropriate here, for the same reasons that it was not appropriate in Sanders.
7028: Duty to assist: whether the Veterans Court properly held DVA did not violate its duty to assist by not obtaining the Western Orthopedics records; the court held the Veterans Court improperly made an initial factual finding on relevance that must be made by the Board, and vacated and remanded.
But that is a finding that must be made in the first instance by a finder of fact, in this case the Board of Veterans' Appeals.
7055: Whether the presumption of competency of VA medical examiners is consistent with the VA's duty to assist and the benefit-of-the-doubt rule; court held it is consistent and narrow.
We see no inconsistency since the "presumption of competency" is far narrower than Francway asserts and is not inconsistent with the statutory scheme.
7370: Whether VA may rely on the service department's roster-based determination without giving the veteran a meaningful opportunity to challenge his service record; court held VA cannot rely on it without such an opportunity and remanded for abeyance pending Corrections Board review.
the VA cannot rely on the service department's determination that the veteran is not on the reconstructed roster without giving the veteran a meaningful opportunity to challenge his service record.
7549: Benefit of the doubt rule under 38 U.S.C. § 5107 and 38 C.F.R. § 3.102: Board need not list each piece of positive and negative evidence; Board properly identified key evidence and assigned probative weight
Similarly, the Board here fulfilled its duty by identifying positive and negative evidence and assigning probative weight in its benefit of the doubt analysis.
8017: Pro-veteran canon of interpretation: court held the canon plays no role where statute is unambiguous, rejecting veteran's reliance on it
Whatever role this canon plays in statutory interpretation, it plays no role where the language of the statute is unambiguous—the situation here.
8390: VA notice duty: whether the evidentiary notice on the claim form was legally sufficient and whether any early-notice error was prejudicial. The court held the generic notice sufficient under Wilson and found any timing error harmless.
we conclude that any error resulting from receiving the notice as part of the claim application form was harmless.
8838: Duty to sympathetically read a pro se CUE motion to discern all potential claims; the Allen concurrence erred in requiring a full legal argument to plead CUE.
Under a sympathetic reading of Mr. Perciavalle's claim, the VA was required to determine all potential claims raised by the evidence, applying all relevant laws and regulations.
9032: Duty to assist: no colorable argument that VA violated its statutory duty to assist by refusing Spanish-language materials or failing to help obtain the veteran's service records.
There was no colorable argument that the VA violated its statutory duty to assist, nor does Ms. Ovalle establish a colorable due process violation.
9050: Pro-veteran canon of construction (Gardner): the Veterans Court erred by failing to consider the pro-veteran canon before resolving interpretive doubt.
once it is clear interpretive doubt remains, as the Veterans Court concluded, the pro-veteran canon of construction must be considered.
9166: Whether due process requires VA to review the merits of the state garnishment order; court held challenges must be heard in the issuing state and VA review is not required.
Thus, any challenges to the garnishment order are properly heard in the state that issued the garnishment order.
9180: Constructive possession of the NAS Update 2014 under the Bell rule; the Veterans Court applied a 'direct relationship' standard instead of relevance and reasonableness, which the Federal Circuit held was an erroneous legal standard tied to the VA's duty to assist.
Accordingly, in requiring a “direct relationship” between the NAS Update 2014 and Mr. Euzebio’s claim, rather than relevance to his claim, the Veterans Court applied a legally erroneous standard.
9200: Presumption of regularity in mailing VA notice of a 1971 rating decision; Board and Veterans Court legally erred in relying on a presumption of mailing absent proof that a decision was made
Absent proof that a decision was made in 1971 on Mr. Williams's claim, we hold the Board and the Veterans Court legally erred in relying on a presumption of mailing.
9338: Board's duty to address a theory of recovery not raised by the claimant (Robinson duty): the record did not sufficiently support the § 3.312(c)(3) theory, so no duty to raise it arose.
The Veterans Court applied the full regulatory sentence and determined that there was no sufficient evidence in this case to trigger the Robinson duty.
9604: Taylor's argument that VA's outreach and notice duties under 38 U.S.C. 6303 are a precondition to enforcing the 5110 effective-date limit is rejected, following Andrews and Rodriguez.
we decline to disturb our precedent under which VA's compliance with § 6303 is not a precondition to enforcing § 5110's claim-filing effective-date limits.
9935: Benefit-of-the-doubt rule under 38 U.S.C. §5107(b): whether the Board correctly applied the rule and properly assigned probative value to evidence; court held the Board did not err in declining to apply the rule.
We do not agree with Mr. Mattox that the Board and then the Veterans Court, in affirming the decision of the Board, committed reversible legal error.
10013: Fair process doctrine challenge to Veterans Court discovery (VA procurement of evidence against the veteran): court found no legal error because the veteran did not explain what improper discovery occurred.
As such, we discern no legal error in the Veterans Court's decision.
10159: Benefit-of-the-doubt rule under § 5107(b): the Board's finding that the June 2015 opinion was more persuasive was not clearly erroneous, so the rule did not apply (for VA).
Hence, the Veterans Court applied the appropriate standard of review, clear error, and properly took account of the Board’s application of the benefit of the doubt rule.
10321: Benefit-of-the-doubt rule: the court held it does not apply when the preponderance of the evidence is against the claimant, following Ortiz, which it said it was bound by. The veteran lost on this point.

As to whether Ortiz correctly held that the benefit-of-the-doubt rule does not apply when "the preponderance of the evidence is found to be against the claimant," 274 F.3d at 1364, this panel is bound by Ortiz.
10443: Whether the Board must address theories of entitlement not raised by the claimant, under the Robinson standard (duty to address theories raised by the claimant or the evidence); court held Regents did not require departing from Robinson, so the Board need not investigate the unraised catarrhal-fever causation theory.

nothing in Regents requires an agency adjudicating a claimant's assertion of entitlement to benefits to do more than Robinson requires, which is to address any theory of relief raised either by the claimant or by the evidence.
10509: Benefit-of-the-doubt rule under 38 U.S.C. § 5107(b): the court held the rule does not apply when the evidence persuasively favors one side, rejecting Lynch's challenge to Ortiz's preponderance formulation and affirming the denial of benefit of the doubt.
As a corollary, evidence is not in "approximate balance" or "nearly equal," and therefore the benefit-of-the-doubt rule does not apply, when the evidence persuasively favors one side or the other.
10700: Duty to assist under 38 U.S.C. 5103A: the court rejected the argument that the VA had to provide additional information, such as underlying scientific data from other veterans' Board decisions, and held the VA's efforts were reasonable.
We reject Mr. Cormier's argument, however.
11322: Whether the Veterans Court's reliance on the medical-treatment truthfulness principle is contrary to the benefit-of-the-doubt rule under 38 U.S.C. 5107(b); court held it is not in conflict.
We determine that the Board's ability to credit statements made for the purpose of medical diagnosis or treatment over other evidence is not in conflict with the benefit-of-the-doubt rule.
11533: Presumption of regularity applied to VA's duty to send a veteran VA Form 21-526 after an informal claim; whether the VA's procedural duty was presumed performed.
the Veterans Court noted that the VA had an undisputed legal duty under 38 U.S.C. § 5102(a) to provide the veteran with VA Form 21-526 when the veteran filed an informal claim.
11816: Fair process doctrine and VA procedural duties to the claimant: assuming without deciding that fair process exists, distinct from due process, and applies in the Direct Review lane, a veteran cannot as a matter of law reasonably expect the Board to delay its decision 90 days after production of the claims file.

we agree with the Veterans Court that a veteran cannot, as a matter of law, establish a reasonable expectation that the Board, when adjudicating an appeal in the Direct Review lane, will, at the veteran's request, delay issuance of its decision for a 90-day period measured from the date of production of the veteran's claims file.
12389: Notice and duty to assist: whether the Board failed to provide notice that the 1969 CUE finding did not entitle the veteran to PTSD compensation; court rejected the argument.
Just because the Board did not expressly reject an argument that Mr. Moore now advances does not mean that the 2015 Board adjudicated a different claim.
13611: Duty to assist: no duty to adjudicate claims reasonably related to the in-service injury under Sellers; VA need not sympathetically read claims
no duty to assist can arise if the VA does not comprehend the condition on which the claim is based.
13921: Benefit of the doubt rule under 38 U.S.C. § 5107(b): whether the RO was required to apply the benefit of the doubt when evidence was undebatably in equipoise
It is undebatable that the RO was required to find in her favor if the evidence was in equipoise, but nothing in the RO's rating decision suggests whether it made that determination.
14318: Whether the 1991 RO decision's explicit denial gave adequate notice under 38 C.F.R. § 3.103 that the related headache claim was implicitly denied, including whether the VA must expressly state reasons for the implicit denial.

Rather, the veteran receives sufficient notice of both the fact of the implicit denial and the reasons therefore when the stated reasons for the explicitly decided claim would reasonably be understood to also extend to the implicitly denied claim.
14358: Pro-veteran canon / benefit of the doubt: court found no interpretive doubt, so the canon did not apply.
Thus, we have no basis to apply the pro-veteran canon of interpretation.
